title: How $20M Lottery Winners End Up Broke in 5 Years

beats.say: Most lottery winners are broke five years later. Not because they bought sports cars.
beats.visual: extreme close-up of a crumpled lottery ticket under sodium streetlight, rain-slick pavement

beats.say: It’s a trap called the obligation spiral. 70% of winners lose it all.
beats.visual: silhouette of hands handing out wads of cash to a crowd, low angle, fog cutting the scene

beats.say: Take Evelyn Adams. She won $5.4M in 1985. Two years later, she was in debt.
beats.visual: extreme wide of an empty casino at night, single practical light casting long shadows

beats.say: Everyone assumed she spent it on luxuries. She didn’t.
beats.visual: close-up of a scattered collection of family photos, receipts, and IOUs on a dark wooden table

beats.say: Adams gave $200,000 to her son for a business. It failed. She gave $1M to her ex-husband.
beats.visual: high angle shot of a check being torn in half, cold fluorescent lighting

beats.say: Then came the aunts, the cousins, the old friends. Each with a story, a need, a dream.
beats.visual: silhouette of a lone figure under a streetlamp, surrounded by outstretched hands, blue hour

beats.say: She couldn’t say no. The guilt was too heavy. The money was gone by 2001.
beats.visual: extreme close-up of a dog-eared tax bill, wet asphalt in the background

beats.say: Why? Because sudden wealth exposes a flaw: most of us don’t know how to handle obligation.
beats.visual: empty highway at night, tail lights fading into the distance

beats.say: We think money changes us. But it reveals us. And for many, that’s the problem.
beats.visual: tower edge against a stormy sky, single human figure in shadow

beats.say: Adams’ last $1.6M went to a failed restaurant. She filed for bankruptcy in 2001.
beats.visual: close-up of a ‘FOR SALE’ sign on a boarded-up building, sodium light

beats.say: The lesson? Money doesn’t fix people. And people don’t fix money.
beats.visual: extreme wide of a quiet suburban street at dawn, no cars, no people

beats.say: Obligation is the hidden tax on windfalls. And it’s costlier than you think.
beats.visual: ridge line with a single figure walking away, fog rolling in

beats.say: Follow for the money rules nobody taught you.
beats.visual: empty underpass, rain-slick surfaces, single light source

caption: 70% of lottery winners lose it all. The trap isn’t cars—it’s people. #moneypsychology #lottery #personalfinance #financialfreedom #obligations
description: Evelyn Adams won $5.4M. Five years later, she was broke. The culprit? Sudden social obligations. A lesson in money psychology.
first_comment: If you won the lottery tomorrow, who’s the first person you’d feel obligated to help?

facts.claim: 70% of lottery winners lose their money within five years
facts.basis: Multiple studies and financial advisories, including the National Endowment for Financial Education (NEFE)

facts.claim: Evelyn Adams won $5.4M in 1985 and filed for bankruptcy in 2001
facts.basis: Documented case studies and news reports on lottery winners

facts.claim: Adams gave $200,000 to her son for a business and $1M to her ex-husband
facts.basis: Interviews and financial records cited in various reports on her spending
